board_fact: The rook on h7 stands on the h-file in front of the queen on h5 with only White's bishop on h6 between them, and that bishop leaves with check.

lesson: When your own piece is the only thing blocking your queen's line to a loose enemy piece, move that piece with check instead of moving the queen.
board_fact: The rook on h7 is loose on the h-file behind White's bishop on h6; Bg7+ and Bf6+ open the line, while Qg6+ takes the queen off the h-file.

lesson: A piece that is defending something and is itself attacked is doing two jobs; trade it off before it fails.
board_fact: The queen on h5 was the only guard of the bishop on h6 and was herself attacked by the queen on f7, and Qxf7 trades those queens off.

lesson: Before you move a piece, check what it is holding.
board_fact: The queen on f7 was the only guard of the pawn on e6, so after she leaves White plays Qf6+ and then takes it.

lesson: When the same check is available from two squares, pick the one that shuts the enemy king in.
board_fact: After Qf6+ the king escapes to h7; Qh6+ first takes that square away, and only then does Qf6+ win the pawn on e6.

lesson: Work out the pawn ending before you offer a queen trade; a pawn down with only pawns left is usually just lost.
board_fact: Qf7 stands right in front of the white queen on c7, and after Qxf7+ Kxf7 only pawns are left with Black one pawn short.

lesson: When you are a pawn up, trading queens usually makes the win easier, not harder.
board_fact: Qxf7+ swaps the queens and leaves White a pawn up with nothing but pawns on the board; Qg3+ kept the queens on.

lesson: With queens still on, leave the pawns next to your own king where they are.
board_fact: After h4 the square h2 is empty and the king on h1 has nothing in front of it, and the black queen heads for h5 and then d1.

lesson: Before you offer a queen trade, count the pawn ending that is left behind.
board_fact: After Qxf3 exf3 the pawn on f3 has no defender and White's king walks over through f2 and takes it.

lesson: In a pawn ending, walk your king forward first; pawns that run ahead alone get stopped.
board_fact: After d5 Black answers e5 and blocks it while White's king stays on f3, whereas b4 and Kf4-e5 marches the king in.

lesson: When you are a pawn up, the extra pawn is the whole advantage, so avoid swapping pawns off.
board_fact: Taking at once with dxe6 Kxe6 removes one pair of pawns, while after e4 two more pairs come off and White ends with only three pawns.

lesson: A check that drops a pawn is still just dropping a pawn; count the guards of the square first.
board_fact: The pawn that gives the check has no guard at all and the white king on f3 simply takes it.

lesson: When a pawn and the king can both make the same capture, the pawn capture usually gains ground.
board_fact: cxd5 leaves a white pawn on d5 that Black has no pawn left to stop, while Kxd5 leaves the other pawn back on c4.

lesson: Push the pawn that cannot be swapped off and make a runner, instead of offering pairs of pawns.
board_fact: After a4 Black plays b6 and a pair comes off on a5; c5 and c6 instead leaves Black with pawns only on a7 and b5, neither of which can touch the c-pawn.

lesson: Never trade off your most advanced pawn; it is the one the enemy king has to keep watching.
board_fact: cxb6+ swaps the far advanced pawn for the one on b6 and the black king takes it back, while c6 keeps that pawn running to c7.

lesson: Before pushing a pawn forward, count how many pieces hit the square and how many of yours guard it.
board_fact: The pawn on e5 is attacked by the pawn on d4 and the knight on f3 but guarded only by the bishop on g7.

lesson: When an enemy pawn is attacked twice and guarded once, take it.
board_fact: Black's pawn on e5 was attacked by the pawn on d4 and the knight on f3 and guarded only by the bishop on g7; d5 let it live.

lesson: Trade off an enemy knight that has reached a square none of your pawns can ever attack, before you start play on the side.
board_fact: Black has no c-pawn and no e6 pawn, so nothing can ever chase the knight on d5; after a5 it jumps to b6, hits the rook on a8, and the pawn on d6 drops.

lesson: Before you make a safety move, check whether your best-placed piece has a jump that wins something.
board_fact: From b6 the knight attacks the rook on a8, and once the rook steps aside the queen takes the pawn on d6.

lesson: A knight parked deep in your position must be traded off; shuffling your other pieces around it only makes things worse.
board_fact: No black pawn can reach d5 to chase the knight away, so after Nb4 White plays Nxf6+ and then takes the pawn on d6.

lesson: Cash in your pressure while it is there instead of spending a move poking at a piece on the edge.
board_fact: After Nxf6+ Bxf6 the pawn on d6 is held only by the queen on d8, and White's queen on d2 has the rook on d1 right behind her.

lesson: A pawn can never guard again the squares it has just walked past.
board_fact: The pawn on e5 was the only black guard of d4 and f4, and after it pushes on, nothing covers those squares and the pawn itself needs the knight on f6.

lesson: If you are the side with the pressure, keep the pieces on; mass trades help the defender.
board_fact: Bd4 lines up in front of the queen on f6, so Black trades on d4 and the queens and both dark-squared bishops all come off.

lesson: Do not attack a weak enemy pawn with a pawn; you only help him swap his weakness off.
board_fact: Black's pawn on e4 was his weak point, attacked by the rooks on d4 and e1, and after f3 exf3 gxf3 it is gone and White's g-pawn with it.

lesson: With two captures to choose from, start with the one that stops the opponent getting a pawn next to your king.
board_fact: After fxe4 Black plays bxa3 and that pawn sits beside the white king on b1; taking with axb4 first removes it.

lesson: Before you move a piece, check whether an enemy pawn covers the square.
board_fact: The pawn on b3 and the rook on d4 both cover a4 and no black piece guards it, so the knight that lands there is just taken.

lesson: Look for the loose enemy piece before you carry on with your plan; it will not wait.
board_fact: The knight on a4 had no defender while the pawn on b3 and the rook on d4 both attacked it; e5 let it escape with a check from c3.

lesson: If one of your pawns is attacked and nobody guards it, settle that before starting something on the other wing.
board_fact: The pawn on d6 was attacked by the pawn on e5 and no black piece guarded it, so exd6 simply wins it.

lesson: Take the free pawn instead of pushing past it; a pawn in hand beats a pawn one square further on.
board_fact: The pawn on d6 had no guard, so exd6 wins it, while pushing to e6 lets Black answer with fxe6.

lesson: When a pawn or a bishop can make the same capture, check which one leaves your bishop's diagonal open.
board_fact: After Bxb3 the bishop covers c4 and d5, while cxb3 puts White's own pawn in front of the bishop on a2, which then sees only b1 and b3.

lesson: Take the pawn that is already attacked while your pieces still point at the rest; a quiet move lets the target get defended.
board_fact: The pawn on f7 could take on e6, and the knight on c3 was also attacking the pawn on d5; Nb5 gave up the attack on d5.

lesson: Before you place a piece, look for the square where an enemy knight would hit two of your pieces at once.
board_fact: From c3 the black knight attacks both e4 and d5, so the rook on e4 must move again and the pawn on d5 has no other guard.

lesson: A pawn one step from promoting ties an enemy rook down, so push it instead of defending elsewhere.
board_fact: After e7 Black's only way to stop the pawn is to put a rook on e8; Rd4 instead let Black take with fxe6.

lesson: Grab the pawn you are already attacking before you reposition a rook.
board_fact: The pawn on f7 could take on e6 and the knight on c3 was attacking the pawn on d5; Rb5 left both of White's pawns standing.

lesson: A pawn that runs ahead with nothing behind it just gets blocked and collected later.
board_fact: After e7 Black's rook sits in front of it on e8 and the pawn never moves again for the rest of the line.

lesson: Before you move a rook along a file, check whether it is the only thing guarding a pawn on that file.
board_fact: The rook on d4 was the only guard of the pawn on d5, which both the knight on c3 and the rook on b5 attack.

lesson: When your attacked piece can take two things, take the one that is unguarded, not the one that is guarded.
board_fact: The bishop on a2 was guarded by the king on a1, so taking it is only a trade, while the pawn on d5 had no guard at all.

lesson: In a rook ending take the free pawn; the extra pawn is what decides the race.
board_fact: The rook on g3 was already attacking the pawn on h3 and nothing guarded it.

lesson: Before you move a pawn, check what it is guarding.
board_fact: The pawn on h7 was the only guard of the pawn on g6, so once it advances the white king on f6 just takes on g6.
